title: NGC 660
caption: The polar-ring galaxy NGC 660, imaged by the Gemini North telescope

recognition.text: Official NSF NOIRLab / Gemini press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: This Gemini North image centers on NGC 660, a polar-ring galaxy in the direction of the constellation Pisces. A ring of gas and stars circles the galaxy, and the scene shows what was left after one galaxy pierced the heart of another.

The ring is not exactly polar. It is tilted about 45 degrees from the plane of the galaxy's disk. Astronomers think it most likely formed about a billion years ago, when NGC 660 interacted with a gas-rich galaxy, stripped away its gas and funnelled it into its own core, setting off a furious burst of star birth.

The massive stars born in that burst lived only briefly before exploding as supernovae, and their shock waves are thought to have triggered more star formation in a chain that continues today. The youngest stars detected in the ring are only about seven million years old. NGC 660 is also unusually rich in gas, and it resolves into hundreds of objects, many of them blue and red supergiant stars.
scale: NGC 660 spans some 40,000 light-years and lies about 40 million light-years away, according to the International Gemini Observatory.

understand.summary: Taken in visible light with the Gemini Multi-Object Spectrograph on Gemini North. The g, r, i and hydrogen-alpha images are shown as blue, green, orange and red respectively.
understand.eye: The hydrogen-alpha filter isolates one particular red glow from hydrogen gas, and the long exposure gathers far more light than the eye could.

explore: The picture was built from exposures through g, r, i and hydrogen-alpha filters, with a total integration time of 1,620 seconds across all of them. The color composite was produced by Travis Rector of the University of Alaska Anchorage.
alt: The polar-ring galaxy NGC 660, shown in a color composite from the Gemini North telescope.
